finding.title: OS Command Injection
finding.trigger: Attacker could send a SIGINT to the parent process
finding.assumptions: The signal handler for SIGINT is set to a default handler that could execute arbitrary code.

parsed.refutation_attempt:
The reported OS Command Injection claim is based on a misunderstanding of the kill() system call. The kill() function does not invoke a shell or execute an external command; it merely delivers a signal to a process. In this program the signal delivered is SIGINT, a fixed, non‑user‑supplied value. The only user‑controlled source of a signal would be an external process sending SIGINT, but that would not cause arbitrary code execution in this process unless a malicious signal handler were installed; the program sets its own handler explicitly (lines 23‑26) and the default handler is a standard one that simply terminates the process. Therefore the conditions for a command injection vulnerability are not met.

Specifically:
- Lines 23‑26 set a custom handler for SIGINT, so the default handler is overridden.
- The sink at line 55 simply sends SIGINT to the parent, which is a predetermined action, not user‑controlled data.
- No path exists from an untrusted source to an executable command, and the signal handler does not call any exec* or system functions.

Thus the finding is refuted.

finding.title: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection')
finding.trigger: Attacker could cause the parent process to receive a SIGINT
finding.assumptions: The parent process might have a signal handler that executes arbitrary code when SIGINT is received.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Identified that the reported source is the SIGINT signal sent by the child process using kill(getppid(), SIGINT) on line 55. This signal originates from an internal program component (the child process) and not from any user-supplied data (stdin, file, network, argv, environment, IPC). The sink in question is the kill() system call, which merely sends a signal; it does not invoke an OS command or execute arbitrary code on its own. Therefore, there is no OS command injection path. The signal handler in the parent could execute arbitrary code, but that would require a separate vulnerability (e.g., unsafe handler implementation) and is not demonstrated by the code fragment. Consequently, the conditions for a confirmed vulnerability (untrusted source, uncontrolled path to dangerous operation, concrete trigger) are not met.

finding.title: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection')
finding.trigger: Attacker could send a SIGINT to the parent process
finding.assumptions: The signal handler for SIGINT might execute arbitrary code if not properly neutralized.

parsed.refutation_attempt: The reported sink is a call to kill(getppid(), SIGINT), which simply sends a signal to the parent process.  The kill() system call does not construct or execute an external command string; therefore it cannot be exploited for OS command injection.  No part of the code performs a command execution (e.g., system(), exec*, popen()) that could be influenced by the SIGINT source.  Consequently, there is no path from untrusted data to a command execution primitive, and the CWE‑772 claim is unfounded.
